opus-5.5.text:
I think it applies much more broadly than people initially expected. When we started working on RadixAttention in SGLang, the motivating cases were fairly obvious: a long system prompt shared across many requests, or few-shot examples that appear at the start of every query. Even there, the savings are significant, because you don't recompute the KV cache for tokens you've already processed.

Once we started looking at real workloads, though, we found shared prefixes almost everywhere.

**Multi-turn chat** is the simplest example. Each new turn contains the whole conversation history so far. Without reuse you reprocess that history every time, and the cost grows with the length of the conversation. With reuse you only compute the new tokens.

**Agents and tool use** are probably the biggest win today. An agent loop calls the model again and again with the same instructions, the same tool definitions, and a trajectory that keeps growing. Most of every call is identical to the previous one. As agents run longer tasks, sometimes hundreds of steps, prefix caching goes from a nice optimization to something you really can't do without.

**Reasoning and search-style generation** benefit too. With tree-of-thought, self-consistency, or sampling many candidates and picking the best, all the branches share the same root. A radix tree is a natural structure for that: you share the trunk and only diverge at the branches.

**Retrieval and long-context workloads** are another case. If many users query the same document, codebase, or knowledge base, you can keep that context's cache and reuse it across users, not just within one session.

**Structured and batch workloads**, like running the same evaluation template over thousands of inputs or extracting data with a fixed schema, share large templates as well.

So my view is that prefix reuse isn't a niche trick. It reflects how LLMs are actually used: programs that call the model many times with mostly overlapping context. The real questions are on the systems side: how to manage the cache under memory pressure, which eviction policy to use, how to schedule requests so cache hits go up, and, as deployments scale out, how to route requests to the machine that already holds the relevant prefix. That's where much of the interesting work is now, and it's also why the major API providers now offer prompt caching as a product feature. The industry has recognized that the opportunity is real and quite general.

r001.rationale: The response says each new multi-turn chat turn contains the conversation history so far, allowing the system to reuse that prefix and compute only the new tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it applies much more broadly than people initially assume. When we started working on RadixAttention in SGLang, the obvious case was multi-turn chat, where every new message shares the entire conversation history with the previous request. But once you look at real workloads, almost everything has shared prefixes.

Take the system prompt. In production, nearly every request to a deployment starts with the same few hundred or few thousand tokens of instructions. That alone gives you a large reuse rate for free. Then there's few-shot prompting, where the examples are identical across requests and only the final query changes. Agent workflows are even more extreme, because an agent calls the model many times in a loop, and each call carries the same tool definitions plus a growing trace of what happened before. Tree search or self-consistency, where you branch out from a common state and sample multiple continuations, is basically prefix sharing by construction.

Even RAG has structure here. People think of retrieved documents as random, but in practice the same popular documents get retrieved again and again, so you still get hits if your cache is organized well.

Where it's weaker is long single-shot batch jobs with fully unique inputs, like summarizing a million distinct documents once each. There you mostly only get the system prompt, which is still something, but it's not the ten-x savings you see in agent or chat traffic.

So my overall view is that prefix reuse is less of a niche optimization and more a property of how LLMs actually get used. The key is that the serving system has to discover sharing automatically, rather than asking the user to declare it, because developers often don't realize how much redundancy their own applications have.

r001.rationale: It explains that in multi-turn chat, each new message shares the conversation history from the previous request.

astra-6.text:
I think it applies quite broadly, though the amount of reuse depends on the application. Prefix reuse means that when multiple requests start with the same text, you can reuse the computation for that shared beginning instead of processing it again every time.

For example, an assistant might have a long system prompt that defines its behavior and available tools. That prefix can be shared across many requests. If several people are asking questions about the same document, the document can also form a reusable prefix. And in a multi-turn conversation, each new turn includes much of the previous conversation, so there’s an opportunity to reuse that work too.

The key is that it has to be a shared prefix, not just similar information somewhere in the request. So how you arrange the prompt matters: putting stable, shared content first and the changing question afterward makes reuse easier. It won’t help every workload equally, but it’s relevant to a pretty wide range of applications.

r001.rationale: It says each new turn in a multi-turn conversation includes much of the previous conversation, creating an opportunity to reuse that computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it applies pretty broadly, because a lot of AI applications share more input context than you might initially expect. For example, requests to the same assistant often start with the same system instructions. If you’re asking several questions about a document, that document can also be a shared prefix. And in a multi-turn conversation, each new request includes much of the previous conversation.

With prefix reuse, you can cache the computation for that shared beginning instead of recomputing it for every request. The benefit depends on how long the shared prefix is and how often it gets reused. It won’t help as much when every request is completely different, but for applications with repeated instructions, shared documents, or ongoing conversations, it can be very useful.

r001.rationale: The response says each new request in a multi-turn conversation includes much of the previous conversation, explaining how later turns reuse earlier history as a shared prefix.
